summary.text: Callisto, daughter of the Arcadian king Lycaon, was a companion of Artemis in the chase who wore the goddess's garb and swore to remain a maid; loved by Zeus and bearing him Arcas, she was turned into a bear and set among the stars as the Great Bear.

Her parentage was already contested in antiquity: Apollodorus records that while Eumelus and others made her Lycaon's daughter, Hesiod called her one of the nymphs, Asius made her a daughter of Nycteus, and Pherecydes a daughter of Ceteus.

story.text: Lycaon, who ruled in Arcadia, had among his many sons a single daughter, Callisto. She became a companion of Artemis in the chase, wore the same garb as the goddess, and swore to her an oath to remain a maid.

Hyginus likewise makes the maiden of the Great Bear Callisto, daughter of the Lycaon who ruled in Arcadia, naming Hesiod as his authority: out of her zeal for hunting she joined Diana and was greatly loved by the goddess for their kindred temperaments.

Zeus loved her and shared her bed against her will. Apollodorus says he came in the likeness, as some tell it, of Artemis, or, as others say, of Apollo; Ovid likewise has Jove take Diana's own form to embrace and overcome the unwilling nymph in his beloved Arcadia. From the union a son was born, Arcas, who would give the land its name.

Who turned Callisto into a bear is disputed. Apollodorus gives one version in which Zeus himself transforms her, wishing to escape Hera's notice, after which Hera persuades Artemis to shoot her — though he adds that others say Artemis shot her for not keeping her maidenhood.

Pausanias, Ovid, and Hyginus instead make Hera (Juno) the transformer, working in jealous rage once she detects the intrigue, with Artemis (Diana) shooting the bear to please her; Hyginus also preserves the further variant that Diana herself changed Callisto for her lost virginity.

When Callisto perished Zeus snatched the babe, named it Arcas, and gave it to Maia to rear in Arcadia, turning Callisto into the star called the Bear; Pausanias has him send Hermes with orders to save the child she carried in her womb. Ovid tells it otherwise: years later Arcas, hunting in the Erymanthian wood, came near to spearing his transformed mother, and Jove averted the crime by bearing both up into the sky as neighboring constellations.

Pausanias cites the Great Bear as the constellation Homer names in Odysseus's voyage from Calypso, but allows the rationalizing alternative that the star is merely named in Callisto's honor, since her grave is still pointed out by the Arcadians. After the death of Nyctimus her son Arcas came to the throne, introduced the cultivation of crops learned from Triptolemus, and after him the land was called Arcadia and its people Arcadians, no longer Pelasgia and Pelasgians.
